tip: Κόσμος (kosmos) means both 'world' and 'people' – γεμάτος κόσμο (gematos kosmo) is literally 'full of world', Greek's normal way to say packed with people.
Παρακολουθήσαμε (parakolouthisame) comes from παρακολουθώ (parakoloutho = watch/follow) – the verb for shows and documentaries, a step more formal than plain βλέπω (vlepo).
'Prefer X to Y' uses από (apo = from), not παρά (para): προτιμάω τις κωμωδίες από τα δράματα (protimao tis komodies apo ta dramata) – you prefer one 'from' the other.
A TV season is a κύκλος (kyklos = cycle): τρεις κύκλους (treis kyklous) = three seasons. Greek shows run in cycles, not seasons.
Το αρχαίο της Επιδαύρου (to archaio tis Epidavrou = the ancient one of Epidaurus) is no ruin – the 4th-century BC theater still hosts plays every summer.
Έπαιζαν (epezan) = 'they were performing' – the ongoing-past form. It puts you inside the unfolding show; a one-off report would use έπαιξαν (epexan).
Σειρά (seira) is both 'row' and 'series': πρώτη σειρά (proti seira) = front row, but a TV show is also a σειρά (seira). Context decides which.
Ανέβασαν (anevasan) is literally 'they raised' – Greek raises a play onto the stage. The same verb ανεβάζω (anevazo) also uploads files.
Το σκηνικό (to skiniko) is the set – the scenery. Η σκηνή (i skini) is the stage itself. Close relatives, different parts of the theater.
Πίνακας (pinakas) covers 'painting' and '(black)board': κάθε πίνακα (kathe pinaka) here means each painting, but in a classroom it's the board.
Photos come out in Greek: βγάζουμε φωτογραφίες (vgazoume fotografies) is literally 'we take out photos'. Παίρνω (perno = take) is the classic wrong-verb slip here.
Πήρα δανεικό (pira daneiko) is literally 'I took (it) on loan' – the everyday way to borrow. The adjective δανεικό (daneiko = lent) carries the borrowing; the verb is just 'take'.
Δυνατά (dynata) means 'strongly' and 'loudly': διάβασα δυνατά (diavasa dynata) = I read aloud, not I read hard. For sound, strong means loud.
Δοκίμια (dokimia) are literary essays – reflective prose. A school essay is an έκθεση (ekthesi). Greek splits what English packs into one word.
Μού κίνησε το ενδιαφέρον (mou kinise to endiaferon) is literally 'it moved the interest to me' – Greek sets interest in motion rather than sparking it.
Greek has no infinitive, so 'before sleeping' needs a full verb: πριν κοιμηθώ (prin koimitho) = literally 'before I sleep' – the 'I' stays inside the verb.
Emphatic 'its own' agrees like an adjective: τους δικούς της χορούς (tous dikous tis chorous) – δικούς (dikous) wears the same ending as χορούς (chorous).
Αγκαλιά (angalia = embrace) is a bare noun doing adverb work: χορεύαμε αγκαλιά (chorevame angalia) = we danced embrace-style – no 'in an' needed.
Καθυστέρησε (kathysterise) is the one-and-done past: the delay happened, complete. An ongoing 'was running late' would be καθυστερούσε (kathysterouse).
English adds 'got' for 'got lost'; Greek packs it into the verb: χάθηκε (chathike) = it got lost. The -θηκε (-thike) ending does the 'got' work.
Λόγω (logo) = 'because of', and it takes the genitive: λόγω της κακοκαιρίας (logo tis kakokairias) – literally 'by reason of the bad weather'.
Αν γίνεται (an ginetai) is literally 'if it happens' – Greek's everyday 'if possible' softener for requests, with no word for 'possible' in it.
Plain από (apo) can't stand before a clause – 'than I expected' needs απ' ό,τι: απ' ό,τι περίμενα (ap' oti perimena).
Μου έκανε εντύπωση (mou ekane entyposi) flips the roles: the quiet 'made an impression to me'. You're the landing spot, as in μου λείπει (mou leipei = I miss it).
Doubling an adverb is how Greek stretches it: σιγά σιγά (siga siga = slowly slowly) = little by little. Same pattern in λίγο λίγο (ligo ligo = bit by bit).
Κάνω παρέα με (kano parea me) is literally 'I make company with' – in Greek, hanging out is company you actively make, not time you spend.
A circle of friends needs no 'of' word: κύκλο καλών φίλων (kyklo kalon filon) – the genitive endings do the job. Reaching for από (apo) is the English reflex.
Μέσω (meso) = via/through, and it takes the genitive: μέσω βίντεο (meso video) = over video – a compact, slightly formal alternative to με (me).
Μπερδεύτηκα (berdeftika) is literally 'I got tangled up' – Greek's normal verb for confusion. Don't calque 'lost in the map' with χάνομαι (chanomai); tangled is the idiom.
Μόλις (molis) has two jobs: 'as soon as' – μόλις προσγειώθηκα (molis prosgeiothika = as soon as I landed) – and 'just/barely'. Context decides which.
Greek days are 'small', not short: οι μέρες ήταν τόσο μικρές (oi meres itan toso mikres). Κοντή (konti = short) is for physical length – days run μικρή/μεγάλη (mikri/megali).
Καιρός (kairos) means both 'time' and 'weather': με τον καιρό (me ton kairo) uses the time sense – 'with time' = over time.
Όσο (oso) + past tense runs two changes in parallel: όσο περνούσε ο καιρός (oso pernouse o kairos) = as time went by – and the feeling shifted with it.
Greek takes decisions instead of making them: πήρα την απόφαση (pira tin apofasi) = literally 'I took the decision'. Κάνω (kano = make) is the wrong verb here.
Με τίποτα (me tipota) is literally 'with nothing' – trades happen 'with' things in Greek, so δεν θα άλλαζα... με τίποτα (den tha allaza... me tipota) = I wouldn't trade it for anything.
Παρά (para) = 'than' when comparing two matching phrases: περισσότερα... παρά (perissotera... para) – about myself than about the country. Plain από (apo) is for comparing nouns.
Θα (tha) + past tense = 'would': θα το ξανάκανα (tha to xanakana) = I'd do it again. The same θα (tha) that builds the future turns past forms into conditionals.
Πως (pos) and ότι (oti) are interchangeable 'that' after belief verbs: πιστεύω πως (pistevo pos) = πιστεύω ότι (pistevo oti). Only the accent separates πως from πώς (pos = how).
Κάθετα (katheta) is literally 'vertically': διαφωνώ κάθετα (diafono katheta) = 'I disagree vertically' – Greek's version of flatly, completely disagreeing.
Στα (sta) + a neuter plural adjective makes adverbs: στα σοβαρά (sta sovara) = seriously, στα κρυφά (sta kryfa) = secretly. One pattern, a whole adverb family.
Ας (as) + verb = 'let's': ας υποθέσουμε (as ypothesoume) = let's suppose. Swap the verb and the particle still carries it – ας πάμε (as pame) = let's go.
Τα βρουν (ta vroun) hides a dummy 'them': τα βρίσκω (ta vrisko = I find them) means to come to terms. The 'them' never refers to anything – it's baked into the idiom.
Greek flips the English order: άσπρο μαύρο (aspro mavro) is literally 'white black', not black and white. Same oversimplification, opposite color order.
Εν πάση περιπτώσει (en pasi periptosei = in any case) preserves ancient Greek's εν + dative, a case modern Greek dropped – it survives only in set phrases like this.
Πολυλογώ (polylogo) is literally 'I many-word' – πολυ- (poly-) glues straight onto verbs. Για να μην τα πολυλογώ (gia na min ta polylogo) = so I don't over-word it: to keep it short.
